Wilfred Smith.narrative: I have put up half the barns and a good share of the houses in this town, and every one of them in timber, because Kettlebridge will not sell us stone at a price a man can pay. I remember what they charged us the year the chapel roof was mended, and I have not forgotten it. I build for the Market Guild and for anyone else with the marks, and I build it square and true. My son Osbert works beside me, though his eye is on the stonework, and I cannot say I blame him.
goals: keep the building work coming in through the Guild
see Osbert settled in a trade with a future
get good stone at a fair price one day
Wilfred Smith.mood: steady, a little sour about stone

relations.name: Hilda Smith
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She mends bones and I mend roofs; between us the town keeps standing.

relations.name: Osbert Smith
relations.label: son
relations.note: Good hands, but he wants the stone trade and that means Kettlebridge, and I have my doubts.

relations.name: Reginald Hobson
relations.label: friend
relations.note: A mason who curses the same price I do; we understand each other.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: patron
relations.note: The Guild pays on time, and she wants the gate-due gone, which would help my trade.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: stone seller
relations.note: He brings the stone and names the price, and I pay it through my teeth.

relations.name: Aldric Marrow
relations.label: reeve
relations.note: He keeps the due that makes every load dearer, and the walls are his to keep.

relations.name: Stephen Hobson
relations.label: friend's son
relations.note: A decent lad, and a good match for my Osbert's company.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: quarryman
relations.note: A Kettlebridge quarryman; they say he cut into the giants' cairn and brought trouble on the trade.

memories.gist: The year the chapel roof was mended, Kettlebridge named a price for stone that took my breath, and I built the whole thing in timber instead.
I built the Guild's new barn in a fortnight with Osbert and two hired hands, and Mercy Abbot paid the full price without a word.
During the Lean Year I took grain from the town store like everyone else and mended the store's roof for nothing, because it fed us.
A beam fell on a hired hand at the Rowan steading and Hilda set his arm while I held him; he was back at work by harvest.
Osbert came home talking of the Kettlebridge masons and their stonework, and I told him stone is dear and timber is honest, and he did not answer.

stances.why: Stone comes dear from Kettlebridge and timber comes from our own woods.
A builder is only as good as the hands he keeps, and I have held a bad wage in my time.
I have paid them and I know what they ask.
Mercy Abbot has never made me wait for my marks.
My father taught me that, and a crooked wall falls and takes a name with it.

Hilda Smith.narrative: I set bones and clean wounds, and the gate guards come to my door when they have been at the outlaws or each other. I learned what I know from my mother and from the chapel sisters, and Sister Alys still sends for me when a hurt is beyond her salves. Wilfred builds and I mend, and the house is quiet enough. I worry about Osbert going among the Kettlebridge masons, but a mother keeps her worries to herself.
goals: keep the guards and the town in one piece
keep peace between the chapel and the old healers

relations.name: Wilfred Smith
relations.label: husband
relations.note: A good man with a long grudge; I let him have it and mend what he breaks.

relations.name: Osbert Smith
relations.label: son
relations.note: He wants the stone trade; I want him to come home with all his fingers.

relations.name: Sister Alys
relations.label: fellow healer
relations.note: She has the salves and I have the hands; we work well together.

relations.name: Sister Elspeth
relations.label: elder sister
relations.note: She keeps the common fire and the calendar, and she does not turn anyone from the door.

relations.name: Joan Hobson
relations.label: midwife
relations.note: Between us we have brought most of this town into the world.

relations.name: Tobin Marrow
relations.label: captain
relations.note: His guards come to me hurt, and he sends them; I will not say more.

relations.name: Walter Stanhope
relations.label: patient
relations.note: A big man with a short temper; I have stitched him twice and told him to keep his fists down.

relations.name: Alwin Wren
relations.label: old healer
relations.note: He knows the old charms and I know the bones; the sisters listen to us both.

memories.gist: I set a guard's arm at the gatehouse after the outlaws threw a stone at him, and he swore at me the whole time and thanked me after.
The Lean Year brought fevers to the town and I went from house to house with Sister Alys until we had no more salve and made more.
Osbert cut his hand to the bone on an adze and I sewed it and told him a builder needs his hands, and he laughed at me.
Wilfred came home from the chapel roof job in a fury over the stone price, and I let him talk it out and poured him cider.
I helped Joan Hobson with a birthing that went hard, and the child lived, and we sat down in the kitchen after and said nothing for a while.

stances.why: A hurt is a hurt, and the Hearth's peace is not mine to break.
What I hear at a sickbed is not mine to carry to the square.
They keep the road clear of wolves and worse, and they come to me bleeding for it.
Wilfred's quarrels are his; my son is mine.
Alwin Wren's charms and my mother's herbs have mended what the sisters' salves could not.

Osbert Smith.narrative: I have built with my father since I was a boy, and I am a good hand with timber, but timber is not what I want to build with. Stone lasts, and the Kettlebridge masons know how to cut and lay it, and I would learn from them if I could get among them. Stephen Hobson feels the same, and we talk about it over a pot. My father says stone is dear; I say a man should learn the trade that lasts.
goals: learn stonework from the Kettlebridge masons
build something grander than a barn
earn enough to keep a household of his own

relations.name: Wilfred Smith
relations.label: father
relations.note: He taught me everything I know and he will not hear of the stone trade.

relations.name: Hilda Smith
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She mends what I break and does not scold overmuch.

relations.name: Stephen Hobson
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We both want more than a wall or a barn, and we talk of going to Kettlebridge.

relations.name: Reginald Hobson
relations.label: master mason
relations.note: He knows stonework, and he curses the Kettlebridge price; I would rather learn than curse.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter
relations.note: He has been to Kettlebridge and back a hundred times; I have thought of asking him to carry a word for me.

relations.name: Ezra Holt
relations.label: quarryman
relations.note: A Kettlebridge quarryman; they say he cut the cairn, but he knows the stone.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: guild head
relations.note: She pays for good work and she wants trade with Kettlebridge; that is where I would go.

memories.gist: My father and I raised the frame of the Guild's barn in a day, and I looked at it and thought it would be gone in fifty years while a stone barn would stand.
I watched the Kettlebridge masons unload dressed stone at the square and lay it true, and I stayed until they were done.
Stephen Hobson and I sat up late with a pot of ale and swore we would learn stonework, and the next morning I went back to the adze.
I cut my hand to the bone and my mother sewed it, and I told her a builder needs his hands and she laughed.
My father came home from the chapel roof cursing the stone price, and I said nothing, because I would have paid it to learn.

stances.why: Timber rots and stone stands, and the masons who lay it will always have work.
My father would keep me from Kettlebridge, but a trade is a trade.
I want to be known for what I build, not for whose son I am.
Stephen and I have talked of it long enough; a man should not go alone.
My father's temper is short on the stone question, and I have to live under his roof.
